tldr: A humanoid loco-manipulation system is proposed that requires no human motion data and uses only two end-effector targets to automatically determine pelvis height and torso orientation online, yielding to external forces to maintain balance.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of OCLO training and deployment. (a) The lower-body policy is trained via reinforcement learning across a 3-stage curriculum covering walking, end-effector reaching with disturbances, and posture adaptation such as crouching and forward leaning. (b) During real-robot deployment, receiving only two end-effector targets from an operator, OCLO generates pelvis height and torso orientation online using an analytic reachability prior and CEM posture refinement, achieving whole-body coordination through arm IK and the lower-body policy via a spring-damper model.
overview:
In humanoid loco-manipulation—where a robot manipulates objects with its end-effectors while standing or walking—a major challenge is determining not just where to move the hands, but how much to lower the pelvis and pitch the torso to support the motion with the whole body. Conventional approaches rely on human motion capture data or require operators to directly specify head and waist postures, making systems complex while remaining poorly suited for flexible tasks.

To tackle this, the authors introduce "OCLO". It completely eliminates human motion data. Given only two end-effector target poses, OCLO instantly computes pelvis height and torso orientation online using an analytic reachability prior based on the robot's own reachable workspace. Furthermore, posture is refined using a policy-in-the-loop sampling method (CEM), and end-effector references are displaced according to external forces via a spring-damper model so the lower body yields in coordination, achieving whole-body compliance.

In simulation, introducing the reachability prior dramatically improved reference acquisition success rate from 37.8% to 77.8%, and posture refinement significantly reduced end-effector orientation tracking error. On a real Unitree G1 humanoid, the robot maintained balance without falling even under strong pushes and pulls to its end-effectors, successfully performing seven loco-manipulation tasks—such as crouched walking and picking up a box from a low surface—commanded solely through two end-effector targets.
contributions: Acquires whole-body compliance and coordinated locomotion without any human motion data or prior demonstrations, relying purely on reinforcement learning with procedural sampling.

Proposes an online posture generation method that computes pelvis height and torso orientation from only two end-effector targets using an analytic reachability prior combined with policy-in-the-loop sampling (CEM).

Achieves whole-body compliance by displacing end-effector references through a virtual spring-damper model in response to external forces, training the lower body to yield smoothly rather than stiffening against disturbances.

Demonstrates disturbance rejection and seven diverse loco-manipulation tasks including crouching on a real compact humanoid (Unitree G1) without requiring waist or head posture commands from an operator.

sections.heading: How do you determine whole-body posture from just hand positions?
sections.summary: When a humanoid performs manipulation tasks, supporting the motion with whole-body posture is challenging. Prior works relied on human motion data or explicit pelvis commands. This work proposes OCLO, a new approach that generates whole-body posture online from only two end-effector targets while compliantly yielding to disturbances.
sections.details:
When a humanoid robot performs tasks while standing or walking, it must determine whole-body posture—such as how much to lower the pelvis and how much to pitch the torso—in addition to end-effector positions. However, most prior studies have relied on human motion capture data to achieve whole-body coordination, leaving them heavily dependent on external tracking devices such as head and chest sensors.

While procedural learning methods without human data exist, many require operators to directly command pelvis height. Under a fixed standing posture, the robot cannot reach targets that are low or far away. Furthermore, maintaining balance while supporting weight or contact forces at the hands requires considering physical stability, not just geometric reachability.

To address this, the authors propose OCLO, a system that decouples posture generation (geometric reachability) from physical body support (dynamical balance maintenance). An analytic reachability prior instantly determines pelvis height and torso orientation from end-effector targets, and policy-in-the-loop sampling refines this posture. Additionally, end-effector references are displaced using a virtual spring-damper model based on external forces, and the lower-body policy complies by crouching, simultaneously achieving whole-body compliance that yields smoothly to external loads.

sections.heading: Differences from prior work: no human data, online posture, and whole-body compliance
sections.summary: Existing methods struggled with relying on human motion data, requiring external posture commands, or failing to adapt to external forces. OCLO addresses all of these simultaneously and stands out as a system demonstrating whole-body coordination on a real humanoid.
sections.details:
This section organizes related prior work along four axes: absence of human motion data, compliance, online posture determination, and real humanoid demonstration.

### Learning from Human Motion and Its Limitations
Many studies (such as OmniH2O, SONIC, and GMT) train humanoid policies to track human motions, requiring human prior data to generate upper-body actions and posture. Other methods like HOMIE and HugWBC eliminate human data through procedural generation, but their postures rely on explicit operator commands, and whole-body compliance is not learned.

### Posture Determination as External Commands
Frameworks like AMO, FALCON, and CEER require root (pelvis) height inputs separate from end-effector commands. While works such as R2S2 and Ego-VCP include posture planners, they require training planners tailored to specific task rewards. In contrast, OCLO determines posture online from end-effector targets alone using a task-agnostic cost function.

### Compliance and Sampling-Based Planning
Compliant control methods based on impedance control (such as FACET and GentleHumanoid) either do not address complete humanoid loco-manipulation or depend on policies distilled from human motion data. OCLO introduces novelty by combining policy-in-the-loop sampling (CEM)—which unrolls and evaluates the learned policy inside simulation similar to model predictive control—with an analytic prior that drastically lowers computational search costs.

sections.heading: OCLO architecture: 3-stage curriculum and online posture generation
sections.summary: OCLO's learned component is a single policy controlling the 15 lower-body and waist joints, while the 14 arm joints are driven by differential inverse kinematics (IK). Compliance is acquired through a 3-stage curriculum, and during deployment, whole-body posture is determined online from end-effector targets using an analytic prior and CEM.
sections.details:
### III-A Interface and Compliance
End-effector targets and forces are defined in a gravity-aligned moving frame $\mathcal{T}$. As a result, lowering the pelvis shortens the relative distance to end-effector targets, making crouching behaviors functional. A virtual mass-spring-damper model is incorporated at each end-effector; upon experiencing an external force $F_{\mathrm{ext}}$, the reference position $x_{\mathrm{ref}}$ displaces from the commanded target $x_{\mathrm{cmd}}$. The arms track this $x_{\mathrm{ref}}$ via damped least-squares differential IK (200 Hz), and the stiffness parameter $k_p$ is randomized and fed into policy observations.

### III-B Procedural Commands and Reward Design
Training uses no motion capture data. Velocity commands, posture commands $c_{\mathrm{post}}=(h,\theta,\varphi)$ (pelvis height, pitch, roll), end-effector targets, and external forces are all sampled procedurally. A portion of end-effector targets are placed at absolute world heights, forcing the lower body to crouch to reach low targets. Rewards consist of a tracking term toward the compliantly displaced end-effector reference (motivating the lower-body policy, which cannot directly actuate the arms, to use the waist and legs to reduce tracking error), a posture-tracking term that replaces upright penalties, and flat-foot gait shaping terms that do not mimic specific reference trajectories.

### III-C 3-Stage Curriculum
Reinforcement learning uses PPO, trained in parallel inside the MuJoCo Warp environment. Stage 1 trains basic walking; Stage 2 adds end-effector reaching and disturbance loads; Stage 3 removes upright constraints and trains tracking of deep crouching and forward-leaning postures. This phased approach safely layers compliance and diverse posture adaptation on top of a stable walking foundation.

### III-D Online Posture Generation (Analytic Prior & CEM)
To determine posture $c=(h,\theta,\varphi)$ from end-effector targets, an analytic reachability prior is first defined. It computes the downward height deficit $\delta$ of the lowest target and the forward reach excess $\eta$ of the furthest target. Pelvis height decreases with $\delta$, while torso pitch increases with both $\delta$ and $\eta$. This prior evaluates in just $0.07\text{ ms}$ on a CPU. To further refine posture, policy-in-the-loop sampling (CEM) can be applied in tandem. Rolling out 64 parallel candidates over a short horizon (1 second) on a GPU or multithreaded CPU from the current state, CEM evaluates candidates using a task-agnostic cost (fall penalties, end-effector errors, joint torques) to select the optimal posture command.

### III-E Two-Point Interface and Hardware Deployment
The operator only needs to hold two hand controllers, requiring no head or pelvis tracking devices. Because the real robot lacks wrist force sensors, external end-effector forces are estimated from motor torques to drive the spring-damper model.

sections.heading: Simulation and real-robot experiments: power of the prior and remarkable disturbance rejection
sections.summary: In simulation, the analytic prior doubled target acquisition success rate from 37.8% to 77.8%, and CEM refinement improved end-effector orientation error. On a real Unitree G1, while ablation baselines failed under heavy pushes and pulls at the hands, OCLO maintained high stability and completed seven practical tasks.
sections.details:
### IV-A Simulation Evaluation Protocol
Using a Unitree G1 model, policies were evaluated across five tasks: walking tracking (Track), base pushes (Base Push), end-effector pushes (EE Push), sustained loading (Sustained Load), and crouched pushes (Crouched Push). Evaluations were conducted across 90 episodes sharing identical random seeds for fair comparison.

### IV-B Effectiveness of Online Posture Generation (Q1)
When using CEM alone without the prior (OCLO (CEM)), the Track task success rate was only 37.8%, because sampling could not transition from an upright stance to a deep crouch within a short time window. In contrast, OCLO (Prior) with the analytic reachability prior reached 82.2%. Adding CEM refinement (Prior + CEM) reduced end-effector orientation error across all tasks (improving from $17.6^{\circ}$ to $11.5^{\circ}$ on Track) while preserving position tracking accuracy. Furthermore, applying this posture module to a pretrained human-data baseline, SONIC, improved success rates on four out of five tasks, confirming its generality.

### IV-C Ablation of Training Signals (Q2)
Comparisons were made against models trained without end-effector target sampling (B1) or without force disturbance sampling (B2). Baseline B1 fell in 96% of Crouched Push trials. Baseline B2 could withstand static loads but failed under sudden disturbances (achieving a 23.3% success rate on Base Push, compared to 62.2% for OCLO). The performance gap widened as disturbance magnitudes increased, demonstrating that force-aware training is critical for dynamic balance recovery.

### IV-D Real-World Experiments (Q3)
Push and pull disturbances were applied to the base and end-effectors of a physical Unitree G1. While all methods showed comparable robustness to base disturbances, striking differences emerged under end-effector disturbances. Under forward end-effector pulls (20–40 N and 50–70 N), B1 succeeded in only 1/10 trials and B2 in 5/10 trials, whereas OCLO (Prior) reliably recovered balance in 10/10 trials. It demonstrated similar dominance under end-effector pushes and lateral pulls. Furthermore, OCLO successfully performed seven loco-manipulation tasks commanded solely via two end-effector targets without any posture commands: crouched walking under an escalator clearance, wiping a low sink, wiping a whiteboard from top to bottom, transporting a cart and a chair, and picking up and turning with a box from a low surface.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook: toward practical humanoids guided solely by hand commands
sections.summary: OCLO achieves whole-body coordination and disturbance robustness from end-effector targets alone, without requiring human motion data or explicit pelvis commands. While challenges remain in foot placement, stride control, and online stiffness adaptation, it represents an important step toward intuitive teleoperation and autonomous humanoid control.
sections.details:
This paper presented and validated OCLO, a system that achieves whole-body humanoid loco-manipulation commanded only through two end-effector targets without using human motion data.

The key insight lies in decoupling task-level end-effector intent from physical whole-body support. An analytic geometric prior instantly determines approximate pelvis and torso posture, while a shared lower-body policy provides dynamic balance and compliance, eliminating the need to retrain policies for different postures.

At the same time, several current limitations were identified:
- The posture interface is restricted to pelvis height and torso pitch/roll, without dynamically optimizing stance width, foot placement, or gait cycle timing.
- Arm redundancy is handled separately via differential IK, which can lead to instability near kinematic singularities.
- On the physical robot, external forces are estimated from motor torques rather than measured by wrist force sensors, and the impedance stiffness parameters remain fixed during execution.

The authors plan to extend posture generation to encompass footstep planning and gait decisions, incorporate dynamic online adaptation of impedance stiffness, and integrate the system with high-level autonomous foundation policies such as vision-language-action (VLA) models.

takeaways: For humanoid whole-body posture generation, an analytic reachability prior based on geometric calculations functions effectively without requiring any human motion data.
When performing model predictive sampling (CEM), using an analytic solution as an initial anchor prevents optimization failures and significantly improves posture quality (orientation error).
Integrating a virtual spring-damper model that displaces target references under external forces into reinforcement learning enables the lower body to autonomously crouch and yield to absorb impacts.

Restricting teleoperation commands to just two end-effector targets removes the need for operators to control head or pelvis posture, reducing operator burden while supporting diverse real-world tasks.
limitations: The posture generation module only controls pelvis height and torso pitch/roll; gait parameters like stance width, step placement, and gait cycle cannot be dynamically adjusted.
Policy-in-the-loop posture refinement (CEM) currently relies on off-board compute, presenting computational resource challenges for continuous real-time execution on embedded hardware.
Because the physical humanoid (G1) lacks 6-axis wrist force sensors, it relies on indirect external force estimation from motor torques, which limits contact detection accuracy near joint limits.
